5027.dloc: Part PHONÉTIQUE, section ACCENT, pp. 23-24 (running heads 'PHONÉTIQUE 23' / '24 ESSAI DE GRAMMAIRE BANDA'; Google Books H1cOAAAAYAAJ, PA23-PA24, full view, US public domain). and whole-book scan (markers PA23, PA24).
5027.prule: Three-level register tone language: every syllable carries its own tone (haut, moyen, bas). Besides the 'accent de hauteur' an 'accent d'intensité' (stress) is posited on 'certaines syllabes des mots'; no positional, weight or morphological rule for it is given anywhere in the grammar, only its effect: unaccented syllables shorten (marked with a breve) and tend to disappear (Bĕleda > bleda, temŏ > tem, marœ̆ > mar).

5027.tone: Three principal tones (haut, moyen, bas); 'chaque syllabe a sa tonalité propre'. Tone is noted only where the word's function in the sentence changes it (the verbal noun joined to the verb raises the tone of the verb vowel: tee fú'fu vs tee fu wa, lobạn gé'gere vs lobạn gere wa, p. 23; grammatical tone again on pp. 27, 83, 90 per the whole-book scan). 5030.dq: In order to show that the SMPM is right-headed with respect to prosody, one would have to demonstrate two things: (1) the final syllable within the word is most prominent; (2) the rightmost word within the phrase is most prominent.
5030.dloc: Hedding 2022 pp. 176–177 and fn. 13; saved. Tone inventory: Eischens & Hedding 2024 §3.3 'Lexical Tone'. Foot headedness: Eischens & Bennett 2025 preprint saved.
5030.prule: No word-stress rule is stated by any first-hand source. Hedding 2022 says the stress pattern of SMPM remains to be determined: final stress is 'plausible' (rising tones are confined to word-final position) but he offers a historical explanation for that restriction 'without appealing to word stress'; at the phrase level neither noun nor adjective is more prominent (phonological phrases possibly unheaded). Eischens & Bennett 2025 posit a bimoraic foot right-aligned to the prosodic word but leave open 'whether feet are taken to be trochaic or iambic', i.e. whether the stressed mora is penultimate or final. The language is a five-tone (H, M, L, LH rising, HL falling) mora-TBU tone language with contrastive phonation.
5030.srule: Not mentioned in Hedding 2022 (§3.5.3, pp. 172–178 read) nor in any later SMPM source read (Eischens & Hedding 2024 §3; Eischens & Bennett 2025 §3.1–3.3; Eischens 2025); no source establishes even a primary word-stress position, so no secondary/rhythmic stress is described.

5031.dq: There are three stress and or pitch patterns in the dialect of Mecha. Pattern One: A word ending in a short vowel has a primary stress and a high pitch on the penultimate ... Pattern Two: Any word ending in a consonant or in a long vowel has a primary stress and a high pitch on the ultimate syllable ... Pattern Three: In any monosyllabic word, the syllable has a primary stress and a high pitch.
5031.dloc: pp. 44-46; grammatical shifts 4.3.2 pp. 46-48 (example table p. 47); dialect basis p. 1; note 21 p. 95; summary p. 70. Habte 2003: pp. 10, 17-18, 35. Dejene 2010: pp. 44-47, 66.
5031.heavy: a word 'ending in a consonant or in a long vowel' (closed final syllable or final long vowel) takes final stress; a word 'ending in a short vowel' takes penultimate stress. Weight is consulted on the final syllable only; a non-final long vowel does not attract primary stress in Wako's data (dè:mán, barbá:de). Dejene 2010 (Wello) differs for consonant-final words, where a non-final long-vowel syllable takes the primary (áatàm).
5031.dflt: penultimate (any word ending in a short vowel)
5031.prule: Primary stress (realised with high pitch) on the final syllable when the word ends in a consonant or a long vowel; on the penultimate when the word ends in a short vowel; monosyllables stressed. Only the final syllable's weight is consulted (dè:mán 'they went' has a long-vowel penult but final stress; barbá:de 'I or he wanted' is penult-stressed because the word ends in a short vowel).
5031.srule: Three degrees of stress (primary, secondary, weak); secondary stress always carries low pitch and falls on syllables preceding the primary: in words ending in a consonant or long vowel (primary on the ultimate) 'on any preceding syllable' - the examples mark every pre-tonic syllable (bìšá:n 'water', ʔìnǰìrá:n 'lice', dè:mán 'they went'); in words ending in a short vowel (primary on the penult) 'on a preceding syllable if there is any' (examples barbá:de, galgála carry no secondary mark). No secondary after the primary in citation forms; no alternating rhythm described.
5031.quote: There are three degrees of stress - primary, secondary and weak stress, and there are two levels of pitch - high and low in Mecha dialect. Stress and pitch are phonetic in the sense that they are predictable from their phonological environments. They also have a grammatical status in the sense that they signal grammatical meanings. 5032.dq: 10.1 Introduction. In this chapter, I describe word stress in Maaloula Aramaic. I will begin by reviewing and revising the word-stress algorithm which has been known since Bergsträsser (1915).
5032.dloc: Ch. 10 'Stress', §10.1 p. 214 and §10.2 'Stress algorithm' pp. 214-216; algorithm (1) p. 214, exception discussion and examples (2)-(3) p. 215, revised moraic algorithm (4) and window statement p. 216
5032.heavy: Final syllable heavy = 'has a long vowel or ends with two consonants or a geminate' (bimoraic; a single final consonant is extrametrical: ray.ˈšay.⟨n⟩, so final CVC is light). Penultimate syllable heavy = bimoraic: long vowel (ḥaẓ.ˈẓū.ra) or closed CVC (ˈṯar.ʕa, ṯi.na.ˈġel.ča). Light = 'the final syllable is CV or CVC, and the penultimate syllable is CV' (p. 215).
5032.dflt: Penultimate in disyllabic words; antepenultimate in words of three or more syllables (rule 4c, p. 216: 'Otherwise stress the penultimate syllable in disyllabic words and stress the antepenultimate syllable in polysyllabic words').
5032.prule: Weight-sensitive stress in a three-syllable window at the right word edge: stress the final syllable if it is bimoraic (long vowel, or closed by two consonants or a geminate; a single final consonant is extrametrical); otherwise stress the penultimate if it is bimoraic (long vowel or closed CVC); otherwise stress the penult in disyllables and the antepenult in words of three or more syllables (regardless of the antepenult's weight). Bergsträsser 1915: XXI and Jastrow 1997: 336 state the same final-if-heavy-else-penult rule; Eid's corpus study adds the light-light antepenult clause.
5032.srule: Not mentioned in Eid 2024 (ch. 10 'Stress', pp. 214-236, read in full; a full-text search of the book finds no secondary or rhythmic stress; p. 15 'has one main stress' is a wordhood criterion only). Earlier first-hand mention, no placement: Bergsträsser 1915 records a 'Gegenton' (counter-stress, marked with the same acute as the main stress) which verb forms with the double object suffix -lle 'almost always' carry, and after which allegro gemination can occur as after a main-stressed syllable; he gives no rule for where it falls.

5040.prule: Mora-counting tone-accent (pitch-accent) system, explicitly not stress: each simple word carries one culminative high tone-accent realized as an invariant H (on an accented long vowel the second mora bears it, giving a rise). In nouns and adjectives the H falls lexically on the final or the penultimate mora, not predictable from word class or meaning; verb roots are lexically accented (H on the root's first vowel) or unaccented (H on the inflectional suffix; final mora of infinitival -etta).
5040.srule: None: the source denies word stress altogether and any primary/secondary gradation ('there is no such gradable distinction in prominence between two or more accented syllables in a word'); a simple word has one high tone-accent, and morphologically complex words (derived nominals, jussive/negative verbs) may carry two or more equal high tone-accents, which are tone-accents, not secondary stresses.

Second, derived complex words have more than one high tone-accent. ... there is no such gradable distinction in prominence between two or more accented syllables in a word. [p. 113] Thus, Wolaitta does not belong to the category of stress languages. ... All lexical nouns and adjectives have only one high tone…

5040.tone: The source rejects the stress analyses of Adams 1983 and Yitbarek 1983 ('Wolaitta does not belong to the category of stress languages', p. 114) on two grounds: the H sits on the second mora of an accented long vowel (a rise; mora, not syllable, is the domain, cf. Hyman 1981 on Somali as a tonal-accent language with an invariant H), and derived complex words carry more than one H with no gradable prominence (p. 113). One H per simple word in citation form; penultimate position takes only H, final position H or (object pronouns only) falling (p. 119). Independent concurrence: Wakasa 2014, Nilo-Ethiopian Studies 19, p. 32: 'Pitch can be used distinctively. There are minimal pairs distinguished only by pitch, such as dooríis ‘he chose’ and dóóriis ‘he piled up’... Where the high pitch is allocated in the word is determined for each conjugated (inflected) form of each word, and the place is not completely predictable', and within an intonation group only the first word realizes its high pitch.

5049.tone: Hashimoto 1971: 7 phonetic / 4 phonological tones; stress mentioned once, as a device explaining the tone change of yang-p'ing (12) and yang-ch'ü (15) to high falling in non-initial position of compounds ('unless the syllable carries primary stress'; 'composite nouns normally carry primary stress on their first syllables'). Chen & Gussenhoven 2015 (JIPA, Shanghai): no stress statement; 'Within a tone unit, the tonal contours of non-initial syllables never surface, and the tone of the first syllable determines the f0 contour for the whole domain' (p. 334), and tonal reductions attributed 'to the lack of phrasal-level prominence'. Wen 2026 (pp. 2-3): 'Shanghai Wu is regarded as having left-headed word stress; the unstressed (i.e., non-initial) syllables undergo tonal deletion, while the underlying tone of the stressed syllable is preserved' (citing Chen 2000, Duanmu 1993, 1995), but for Shaoxing Wu 'no independent acoustic correlates of stress beyond tonal patterns themselves' (p. 111) and the stress account is called circular. Zhang 2006 (Shaoxing): 'every word has a stress' realised as a full tone on a bimoraic syllable (p. 46); words and feet right-prominent/iambic (p. 230).

5051.prule: No stress statement exists for Wuthathi itself. The only first-hand Wuthathi source (Seligmann & Pimm 1907 'Otati' vocabulary, c.400 words from one speaker, no accent marks, an 'Orthography' paragraph on vowel and digraph values only) says nothing about stress or accent. Crowley 1983's rule for 'the Uradhi dialects' (primary stress on the antepenultimate syllable in words with only short vowels, hence initial in words of three syllables or fewer; every long vowel takes primary stress wherever it stands, so a word may carry two primary stresses) nominally covers Wudhadhi, which Crowley places inside his Uradhi language (p.310), but it rests on his Atampaya, Angkamuthi and Yadhaykenu field data only; every example is Atampaya, Wudhadhi is extinct and was known to him from 'three wuðaði vocabularies', and he states (p.315) that no phonetically accurate published source exists for any dialect but Uradhi proper (Hale). 5052.tone: Lexical word tone: 'There is no lexically contrastive stress in Wutung, but there is word tone. This operates by one of four melodies extending across the word and being realised in various ways depending on the number of syllables and the location of a pitch-attracting ‘accent’.' (App. A.2 p. 354). Ch. 5: melodies H, L, HL, LHL; 'all words bear either no accent, an accent on the first, or on second syllable' (§5.5.1.2 p. 165; §3.6 p. 91 says instead 'always present on the second syllable of polysyllabic words', a minor internal tension). The accent is a tonal-association device only: 'stress is not audibly present on the second syllable any more than on any other syllable. Nor has any acoustic evidence for this accent been found, either in terms of length or amplitude.' §5.1 p. 153: 'stress, which is not lexically contrastive (and seems able to vary freely)'.

affix_stress.q: While stress is not phonemic in Wutung (§3.6), words may be identified on the basis that they may only bear a single occurrence of primary stress, even though the location of this stress is not fixed. Compound verbs bear a single instance of primary stress, identifying them as single words.

tn.quote: Wutung tone is lexical, the domain of operation of phonemic tone being the whole word, with tone ‘melodies’ applying to the entire word and being realised as pitch levels on each syllable. There are four tonal melodies, H (high), L (low) and HL (fall, comprising the sequence [h-l] attached to a single syllable) and LHL (comprising the sequence [l-h-l]). ... While the tone-bearing unit is the word, the level at which the surface pitches are realised is the syllable.
tn.cite: Marmion, Douglas Edric. 2010. Topics in the phonology and morphology of Wutung. PhD thesis, The Australian National University, Canberra.
tn.note: Four word-tone melodies (H, L, HL fall, LHL) built from [h]/[l] elements, mapped left-to-right with an optional tone-attracting accent; no tonal morphemes; stress non-contrastive and free-varying.
